summary:
Cauca department stands under Colombia's national framework for sexual-orientation and gender-identity law. The sources assembled for this record contain no Cauca-specific statute, court ruling or documented incident: Human Rights Watch's Colombia country page records no finding for Cauca, and the CNN 'As Equals' follow-up of 6 August 2025 on killings of LGBTQ+ people (https://www.cnn.com/2025/08/06/americas/colombia-lgbtq-attacks-sara-millerey-as-equals-intl-latam) describes no incident in the department. What a trans visitor faces in Cauca is therefore the national floor, plus the national patterns of violence that the sources place across the country's departments.

That floor is comparatively developed. Consensual same-sex relations have been legal since 1981; Congress passed a national ban on discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation in 2011; the Constitutional Court legalised same-sex marriage in April 2016, with the country's first same-sex wedding taking place in Cali on 24 May 2016; and adoption by same-sex couples has been available since 2015.

Legal gender recognition rests on self-recognition, a basis recognised in Constitutional Court jurisprudence dating from 1993 and carrying no surgical requirement. Since a rule change approved in June 2015, trans Colombians change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments. Birth certificates offer F, M, NB and T markers, and national identification documents have carried 'trans' and 'non-binary' markers since November 2025.

Entry and partner recognition are settled in the visitor's favour. The first same-sex marriage conducted abroad was registered in Colombia in March 2016, and the National Registry issued a memo ordering all notaries and registrars to register same-sex marriages performed outside the country. Same-sex couples married abroad are entitled to the same visa, healthcare benefits, inheritance and pension rights as heterosexual spouses once they present a stamped marriage certificate and identification papers at the nearest designated office.

Access to premises and to detention facilities is covered by court order and administrative decree. Judgments T-314 of 2011 (Tequendama Hotel), T-909 of 2011 (Cosmocentro mall guards in Cali) and T-301 of 2004 (Santa Marta police at the city boardwalk) protect entry to public and commercial premises. A 2011 Constitutional Court ruling allowed a transgender woman prisoner to choose her own hairstyle and makeup, and a Colombian court has since issued a ruling on the treatment of trans detainees.

The violence picture is the part of the assessment that carries real weight for a visitor. The pattern of armed-group 'social cleansing' campaigns documented in neighbouring departments applies to Cauca, and the national kill figures apply: 41 transgender women were killed in 2023, eight between February and April 2024, and 13 trans people in the first quarter of 2025, with the Attorney General's Office recording 35 LGBTI murders between January and May 2025. Sara Millerey, 32, drowned in a creek outside Medellín in Bello, Antioquia on 5 April 2025 after being thrown in unable to swim with fractured legs, arms and hands; her mother Sandra Borja said: 'They killed her for being who she was.' Reporting after that case describes gangs linked to queer and transgender deaths and killings that did not stop in its wake.

Protection machinery exists but has not closed the gap. In July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, the state acknowledging conflict-driven violence as gender persecution, a crime against humanity, and the UN Human Rights Committee noted concern. In May 2025 the UN Independent Expert on SOGI violence and discrimination, Graeme Reid, concluded a fact-finding mission across multiple Colombian cities, praising the government's legal reforms while warning of a stark disconnect between institutional progress and daily lived experience, with widespread discrimination and violence requiring urgent attention as killings rise.
tangentialFactors:
The most detailed account of armed-group targeting in the region comes from Caquetá department, immediately adjacent to Cauca. The Guardian of 30 July 2024 (https://www.theguardian.com/global-development/article/2024/jul/30/lgbtq-homophobia-social-cleansing-trans-women-caqueta-colombia-targeted-armed-groups) reported flyers on the streets and via WhatsApp naming 'faggots, lesbians and men and women who destroy homes' as legitimate military targets. Three armed men told a trans woman and local election candidate she had one week to leave town; she hid for a week, then fled at night. A second trans woman said a friend was killed. Discrimination there limits trans women mainly to hairdressing or sex work. The incidents described occurred in Caquetá, not Cauca.

Comparable lists circulate elsewhere. In Guajira, armed groups have posted flyers carrying a kill list of named individuals since March 2024, stating that 'all will be military targets... homosexuals, lesbians, rapists, trans'. These campaigns, together with the national kill figures, are the basis for treating the pattern as applying to Cauca rather than to any single department.

The conflict context is national and decades long. Killings of queer Colombians continued after the Millerey case, described in reporting as calculated brutality persisting amid the country's civil conflict, and the transitional-justice indictment of July 2023 arose from that same record.
localsOnly:
Resident trans Colombians change the sex marker on identification by signing a document before a notary, a route available since the rule change approved in June 2015 and preceded by Constitutional Court jurisprudence from 1993 recognising self-recognition without a surgical requirement. Birth certificates carry F, M, NB and T markers; national identification documents have carried 'trans' and 'non-binary' markers since November 2025.

The 2016 Ministry of Interior decree set procedural obligations for government institutions covering LGBTI rights in public education, health care, prisons and as victims of armed conflict. A May 2018 executive decree by President Juan Manuel Santos extended guarantees to housing, work, recreation, sports and culture.

Employment discrimination narrows the options available to trans women, with reporting indicating that hairdressing and sex work remain the main avenues open to them. Trans women standing for office have been among those threatened: in Caquetá a trans woman and local election candidate was given one week to leave town by armed men and ultimately fled at night.

Detention is governed by court order. A 2011 Constitutional Court ruling allowed a transgender woman prisoner to choose her own hairstyle and makeup, and a Colombian court has since issued a ruling on the treatment of trans detainees.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Cauca-specific legal provision, administrative order or court judgment appears in the sources for this record, and no incident of violence against a trans person in Cauca is documented here. Whether the national framework is applied in practice by notaries, police and health facilities in Cauca is unresolved on these sources.

Implementation of the 'trans' and 'non-binary' national identification markers, introduced in November 2025, has not been verified for Cauca's registration offices; the sources record the national introduction only.

The armed-group 'social cleansing' material available for this assessment comes from Caquetá and Guajira. Its presence in Cauca is inferred from national patterns rather than documented by a Cauca source, and remains unresolved.

The Guardian material (https://www.theguardian.com/global-development/article/2024/jul/30/lgbtq-homophobia-social-cleansing-trans-women-caqueta-colombia-targeted-armed-groups) attributes specific threats to Caquetá; those incidents should not be read as Cauca events. Human Rights Watch's Colombia page (https://www.hrw.org/americas/colombia) yields no documented finding for Cauca.
